title: Seating Chart for Round Tables: How Many Fit + How Many Tables You Need
description: How many people fit at 48, 60 and 72-inch round tables, how many tables you need for 50 to 250 guests, room space per table, and how to seat round tables without splitting families.
h1: Seating chart for round tables: capacity, table count and layout
lead: Round tables are the default at weddings and b'nai mitzvah because everyone can talk to everyone. The catch is the math: how many people actually fit, and how many tables you need.

howto.name: How to plan a seating chart for round tables

steps.name: Pick the table size
steps.text: Choose 60-inch rounds (8-10 guests) or 72-inch rounds (10-12) with your venue.

steps.name: Count the tables
steps.text: Divide confirmed guests by comfortable seats per table, round up and add one spare.

steps.name: Check the room
steps.text: Allow roughly a 10-12 foot square per 60-inch table including chairs and aisles, and confirm with the venue's floor plan.

steps.name: Seat parties, not people
steps.text: Fill tables with whole couples and families, using 9 or 11 seats where a group doesn't divide evenly.

body_html:
How many people fit at a round table?

Published capacity charts agree on the range, and differ on how tight is acceptable. These are the figures rental companies and planners typically use:

Round table capacity
TableComfortableMaximum (tight)Good for
48-inch (4 ft) round68Small rooms, kids’ tables, cocktail areas
60-inch (5 ft) round810The standard wedding table
66-inch round911Venues that want 10 without crowding
72-inch (6 ft) round1012Big families, fewer tables to fill

Sources: Chiavari Chair Sales (60-inch comfortably seats 8; 72-inch 10–12), Party Rental Ltd. (60-inch 8–10; 72-inch 10–12) and Designing Idea. Chiavari chairs are narrower than banquet chairs, so venues using them often fit the higher number; big centerpieces and chargers push you toward the lower one. Always ask the venue what they set.

How many round tables do you need?

Tables = guests ÷ comfortable seats per table, rounded up, plus one spare. The spare absorbs late RSVPs and groups that don’t divide neatly. Don’t count the head or sweetheart table in the division.

Number of round tables by guest count
Guests60″ at 860″ at 1072″ at 1072″ at 12
507 + 15 + 15 + 15 + 1
8010 + 18 + 18 + 17 + 1
12015 + 112 + 112 + 110 + 1
15019 + 115 + 115 + 113 + 1
20025 + 120 + 120 + 117 + 1
25032 + 125 + 125 + 121 + 1

Notice the trade-off: 72-inch tables at 12 save tables (and centerpieces, linens and floor space), but conversation across a 6-foot table is harder. Many couples mix sizes: 72-inch rounds for big family tables, 60-inch for friend groups.

How much room do round tables take?

A seated guest needs roughly 18–24 inches behind the table edge for the chair and to stand up, and servers need an aisle on top of that. A practical planning figure is a square of about 10–12 feet per 60-inch table and 11–13 feet per 72-inch table, including chairs and walkways. That is a rule of thumb only: the venue’s floor plan and fire-code capacity are what count, along with the dance floor, the buffet or bar lines and any accessible routes.

Seating round tables without splitting families

Round tables punish odd numbers. A family of 5 and a couple make 7, which leaves one awkward seat at a table of 8. Some fixes that work:

  • Seat parties, not people. Work in invitations (a couple, a family of four) and fill tables with whole parties. Never split a couple to make the numbers work.
  • Allow 9 or 11. A 60-inch round set for 9 or a 72-inch set for 11 looks normal and solves most leftovers. Tell the venue the per-table count in advance.
  • Use the spare table for overflow. Three couples who know each other loosely make a better table than six seats scattered across the room.
  • Keep the empty seat away from the dance floor. If a table has one empty seat, put it where it faces the couple, so nobody sits with their back to the action.
  • Kids’ tables can be smaller. A 48-inch round with 6 kids plus booster seats is easier than squeezing 10 children around a 60-inch table.

Example: 130 guests on 60-inch rounds

130 guests ÷ 10 = 13 tables, plus one spare = 14 rounds, and a sweetheart table. In practice, groups won’t divide into exact tens, so a typical result looks like: 9 tables of 10, 3 tables of 9, 1 table of 8 and a spare with 5 late RSVPs. That’s still 14 rounds, and nobody is split from their partner.

Round tables vs. long tables

Long (banquet or farm) tables seat more people in the same floor area and look great for a family-style dinner, but you can only talk to the three or four people near you. Rounds are more social and easier to assign by group. Many venues mix both: a long head table and rounds for everyone else. Our seating chart maker supports both round and long tables, shows seats used per table, and auto-seats guests by group so you can try both layouts in a few minutes.

faq.q: How many people can sit at a 60-inch round table?
faq.a: Usually 8 comfortably and up to 10. Rental companies list it at 8-10; venues using slim Chiavari chairs often seat 10.

faq.q: How many people fit at a 72-inch round table?
How many round tables do I need for 150 guests?
faq.a: At 10 per 60-inch table, 15 tables plus one spare. At 8 per table, 19 plus a spare. At 12 per 72-inch table, 13 plus a spare.

faq.q: Is it OK to have 9 people at a table?
faq.a: Yes. Odd counts like 9 or 11 are common and are better than splitting a couple or family. Tell the venue the count per table so place settings match.
